claim: NSF is a highly conserved AAA+ protein that disassembles SNARE complexes.
source: A highly conserved AAA+ protein, NSF (N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor) and an adaptor protein, SNAP (soluble NSF attachment protein), disassemble the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: SNAP is an adaptor protein that works with NSF to disassemble SNARE complexes.
source: A highly conserved AAA+ protein, NSF (N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor) and an adaptor protein, SNAP (soluble NSF attachment protein), disassemble the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The neuronal SNARE complex is composed of syntaxin-1A, synaptobrevin-2, and SNAP-25A.
source: We report electron-cryomicroscopy structures of the complex of NSF, αSNAP, and the full-length soluble neuronal SNARE complex (composed of syntaxin-1A, synaptobrevin-2, SNAP-25A) in the presence of ATP under non-hydrolyzing conditions at ~3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The 20S complex structures were determined at approximately 3.9 Å resolution.
source: We report electron-cryomicroscopy structures of the complex of NSF, αSNAP, and the full-length soluble neuronal SNARE complex (composed of syntaxin-1A, synaptobrevin-2, SNAP-25A) in the presence of ATP under non-hydrolyzing conditions at ~3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by Table 1.

claim: Two αSNAP molecules interface with a specific surface of the SNARE complex through electrostatic interactions.
source: These structures reveal electrostatic interactions by which two αSNAP molecules interface with a specific surface of the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in Figure 5B.

claim: The 15 N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A are loaded into the D1 ring pore of NSF.
source: This interaction positions the SNAREs such that the 15 N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A are loaded into the D1 ring pore of NSF via a spiral pattern of interactions between a conserved tyrosine NSF residue and SNAP-25A backbone atoms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in Figures 2C and 9.

claim: A conserved tyrosine residue in NSF interacts with SNAP-25A backbone atoms in a spiral pattern.
source: This interaction positions the SNAREs such that the 15 N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A are loaded into the D1 ring pore of NSF via a spiral pattern of interactions between a conserved tyrosine NSF residue and SNAP-25A backbone atoms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in Figure 9C.

claim: Substrate loading likely precedes ATP hydrolysis.
source: This loading process likely precedes ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the non-hydrolyzing conditions used in the experiments.

claim: ATP hydrolysis drives complete disassembly of the SNARE complex.
source: Subsequent ATP hydrolysis then drives complete disassembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by functional assays in Figure 10.

claim: The neuronal SNARE complex is an exceptionally stable four-helix bundle.
source: This process has been studied extensively in the context of neurotransmission, where synaptic vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane is driven by the formation of the ternary neuronal SNARE complex, an exceptionally stable four-helix bundle composed of syntaxin, synaptobrevin, and SNAP-25 (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NSF and SNAPs form the 20S complex with the cis SNARE complex.
source: After fusion, NSF—together with several molecules of an adaptor protein, SNAP (Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment Protein)—binds to the cis SNARE complex, forming the so-called 20S complex and disassembles it in an ATP-dependent manner (Hanson et al., 1997; Mayer et al., 1996; Söllner et al., 1993; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NSF disassembles the SNARE complex in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: After fusion, NSF—together with several molecules of an adaptor protein, SNAP (Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment Protein)—binds to the cis SNARE complex, forming the so-called 20S complex and disassembles it in an ATP-dependent manner (Hanson et al., 1997; Mayer et al., 1996; Söllner et al., 1993; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Free SNARE proteins are recycled after disassembly for additional rounds of synaptic vesicle formation and fusion.
source: The free SNARE proteins are then recycled and used for additional rounds of synaptic vesicle formation and fusion (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007; Miller et al., 2011; Mossessova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NSF and SNAPs are part of a quality control system with Munc18 and Munc13 that ensures proper trans SNARE complex assembly.
source: Moreover, together with Munc18 and Munc13, NSF and SNAPs are part of a quality control system that ensures proper trans SNARE complex assembly (Lai et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NSF is composed of an N-terminal domain and two ATPase domains (D1 and D2).
source: NSF is composed of an N-terminal domain (N) and two ATPase domains (D1 and D2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Six NSF molecules form a two-layer ring structure regardless of nucleotide state or substrate presence.
source: Regardless of the nucleotide state or the presence of substrate, six NSF molecules form a two-layer ring structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior cryo-EM studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: The D2 ring of NSF is nearly perfectly six-fold symmetric in all structures determined.
source: While the D2 ring is nearly perfectly six-fold symmetric in all structures determined thus far, the conformation of the D1 ring changes substantially depending on its nucleotide state.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies.

claim: The conformation of the D1 ring changes substantially depending on its nucleotide state.
source: While the D2 ring is nearly perfectly six-fold symmetric in all structures determined thus far, the conformation of the D1 ring changes substantially depending on its nucleotide state.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies.

claim: In the ADP-bound state, the D1 ring is in an open flat-washer conformation.
source: These conformational changes are likely related to those sampled during substrate processing; in the ADP-bound state, the D1 ring is in an open flat-washer conformation, while the ATP-bound D1 ring further separates and forms a split-washer conformation (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: The ATP-bound D1 ring forms a split-washer conformation.
source: These conformational changes are likely related to those sampled during substrate processing; in the ADP-bound state, the D1 ring is in an open flat-washer conformation, while the ATP-bound D1 ring further separates and forms a split-washer conformation (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: In the 20S complex with AMPPNP, the D1 ring largely recapitulates the split-washer configuration.
source: Structures of the 20S complex in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMPPNP largely recapitulate the split-washer configuration of the D1 ring (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: In the neuronal 20S complex, the SNAREs are positioned nearly coaxially above the D1 ring with N-termini near the D1 pore.
source: In the case of the 20S complex formed with the neuronal SNARE complex, the SNAREs are positioned nearly coaxially above the D1 ring, with the N-termini of the SNAREs in the vicinity of the D1 pore.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: The N domains, αSNAPs, and SNAREs form a 'spire' on top of the D1 ring.
source: Together, the N domains, αSNAPs, and SNAREs form a 'spire' on top of the D1 ring.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies.

claim: The number of αSNAPs in previous 20S structures varied based on the particular SNARE proteins used.
source: In terms of substrate recognition, for example, the number of αSNAPs varied based on the particular SNARE proteins used—the structure of the V7-20S complex, composed of NSF, αSNAP, Vamp7, the full cytoplasmic region of syntaxin-1A including the Habc domain, and full-length SNAP-25A contained only two αSNAPs, whereas the structure of the 20S complex composed of NSF, αSNAP, the full cytoplasmic region of synaptobrevin-2, a cytoplasmic fragment of syntaxin-1A without the Habc domain, and the two SNARE motifs of SNAP-25A included four αSNAPs (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to prior structural studies (Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: Previous 20S structures did not permit assignment of specific SNARE proteins in the four-helix bundle density.
source: However, in all of these 20S structures, the local resolution of the reconstructed maps did not permit assignment of the specific SNARE proteins in the density associated with the four-helix bundle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing limitations of prior studies.

claim: No interaction between the SNAREs and the D1 ring of NSF could be observed in previous structures.
source: Furthermore, no interaction between the SNAREs and the D1 ring of NSF could be observed, leaving questions related to substrate recognition and processing unanswered.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing limitations of prior studies.

claim: 3D classification of the 20S complex produced four classes, two of which contain all components.
source: 3D classification produced four classes, two of which (Classes II and IV) contain all components of the 20S complex, while Classes I and III are not well resolved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Refinement of Class IV yielded two reconstructions (FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2) at 4.4 Å resolution.
source: Refinement of the class that appears to have the best-resolved density for the entire 20S complex (Class IV) without symmetry restraints yielded two reconstructions of 20S complexes (FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2 at 4.4 Å; Figure 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: A tube of density runs from the SNARE complex to the center of the D1 ring of NSF, suggesting direct engagement of substrate.
source: Most importantly, a tube of density runs from the SNARE complex to the center of the D1 ring of NSF, suggesting direct engagement of substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Focused refinement yielded two classes of complexes with near-atomic resolution (FL-20Sfocus-1 at 3.8 Å and FL-20Sfocus-2 at 3.9 Å).
source: To improve the detail of the reconstruction, focused refinement (see Materials and methods) was performed, in which all but the NSF D1 and D2 domains was masked; this approach yielded two classes of complexes with near-atomic resolution (FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2, 3.8 Å and 3.9 Å, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: The focused reconstructions show well-resolved density for secondary structure and side chains.
source: The focused FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2 classes show well-resolved density for a variety of features, including secondary structure and side chains (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: In both FL-20S classes, the NSF D1 and D2 ATPase domains form a pair of stacked, hexameric rings.
source: In both FL-20S classes, the NSF D1 and D2 ATPase domains form a pair of stacked, hexameric rings, with N domains, αSNAP, and soluble neuronal SNARE complex forming a spire-like structure on top (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The D1 ring forms an asymmetric split-washer in which the six D1 domains undergo a rigid-body transformation in a spiral pattern.
source: While the D2 ring is largely six-fold symmetric, the D1 ring forms an asymmetric split-washer in which the six D1 domains of protomers A–F undergo a rigid-body transformation in a spiral pattern (average rotation of 57.5° ± 1.0° about the principle axis), with each consecutive counter-clockwise step away from the domain closest to the D2 ring (protomer A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The average rotation between consecutive D1 domains in the spiral is 57.5° ± 1.0°.
source: While the D2 ring is largely six-fold symmetric, the D1 ring forms an asymmetric split-washer in which the six D1 domains of protomers A–F undergo a rigid-body transformation in a spiral pattern (average rotation of 57.5° ± 1.0° about the principle axis), with each consecutive counter-clockwise step away from the domain closest to the D2 ring (protomer A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Density corresponding to the D1 domain of protomer F is poor and not of sufficient quality to permit backbone tracing.
source: While the D2 domain of protomer F is clearly defined, density corresponding to its D1 domain is poor and not of sufficient quality to permit backbone tracing, implying substantial conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The small D1 subdomain of protomer F is rotated in a more pronounced fashion than those from the other protomers.
source: Moreover, the small D1 subdomain of protomer F is rotated in a more pronounced fashion than those from the other protomers (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both FL-20S classes reveal a spire in which the N-terminal end of the SNARE complex is positioned over the D1 ring by two αSNAP molecules.
source: Regarding substrate loading, both FL-20S classes reveal a spire in which the N-terminal end of the SNARE complex is positioned over the D1 ring by two αSNAP molecules, each of which is in turn bound by two N domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The map quality permits explicit assignment of the four SNARE α-helices and determination of the absolute orientation of the SNARE complex.
source: Critically, and in contrast to previous studies, the map is of sufficient quality to permit explicit assignment of the four SNARE α-helices and thus the determination of the absolute orientation of the SNARE complex in the FL-20S complex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Each SNARE helix is individually resolvable in the density.
source: Each helix is individually resolvable, and a rigid body fit of the structure of the crystal structure of the neuronal SNARE complex (Sutton et al., 1998) places it in an orientation which properly accounts for the curvature of the bundle.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SNARE complex assignment is corroborated by the presence of a low-resolution feature matching the position of syntaxin-1A F216 in the asymmetrical −3 layer.
source: This assignment is corroborated by the presence of a low-resolution feature that approximately matches the position of syntaxin-1A F216 in the asymmetrical −3 layer of the SNARE complex (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reconstructions do not show any sign of intercalation by αSNAP residues into the SNARE complex.
source: These reconstructions do not show any sign of intercalation by αSNAP residues into the SNARE complex as had been previously proposed based on a lower resolution reconstruction (Zhou et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and contradicts a previous proposal.

claim: The assignment of SNARE complex components is supported by sidechain densities of the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A.
source: The assignment of the SNARE complex components is also supported by sidechain densities of the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A (Figure 2C) and by the presence of diffuse density consistent with the linker that connects the two SNAP-25A SNARE motifs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2C and 7.

claim: Diffuse density consistent with the SNAP-25A linker is present, suggesting it samples multiple conformations.
source: This study for the first time provides structural information about the location of the SNAP-25A linker, albeit at low resolution; although the weak density suggests that it samples multiple conformations, these data show that it is at least partially associated with the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The primary αSNAP interfaces are formed through electrostatic interactions between positively charged αSNAP surfaces and a complementary negatively charged SNARE surface.
source: The primary αSNAP interfaces are formed through electrostatic interactions between two positively charged αSNAP surfaces and a complementary, negatively charged surface formed by the SNARE motifs of synaptobrevin-2, syntaxin-1A, and the second SNARE motif of SNAP-25A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The electrostatic surface distribution on SNARE complexes is highly conserved, suggesting a general principle for SNAP recognition.
source: This electrostatic surface distribution is highly conserved for all SNARE complex structures determined to date (Diao et al., 2015), suggesting a general principle for SNAP recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The more neutral first SNARE motif of SNAP-25A is largely exposed, facing the D1 ring split.
source: This SNARE surface is oriented away from the D1 pore; in contrast, the more neutral first SNARE motif of SNAP-25A is largely exposed, facing the D1 ring split.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The spire orientation varies by a discrete rotation about the hexamer axis between FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2 classes.
source: While both FL-20S classes show clear density for the spire, its orientation varies by a discrete rotation (if viewed from the D1 end, counter-clockwise) about the hexamer axis as well as a slight translation in the hexamer plane away from the split in the D1 ring in each (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In FL-20S-1, protomers A and B engage one αSNAP, while protomers C and D engage the other.
source: In the first class, protomers A and B engage one αSNAP, while protomers C and D engage the other (Figure 3C, left).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In FL-20S-2, the N domain is shifted by one protomer counter-clockwise, with domains B and C engaging the first αSNAP and domains D and E engaging the second.
source: In the second class, the N domain is shifted by one protomer counter-clockwise about the hexamer axis, with domains B and C engaging the first αSNAP and domains D and E engaging the second (Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference in spire configuration between FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2 results in a 53.2° rotation of the αSNAPs and SNARE complex about the hexamer axis.
source: This difference results in a 53.2° rotation of the αSNAPs and SNARE complex about the hexamer axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Despite variation in spire configuration, there is little difference in the interaction between SNAP-25A and the D1 pore or in the overall configuration of the D1 and D2 domains of protomers A–E.
source: Despite the variation in spire configuration between these classes, there is little difference in the interaction between SNAP-25A and the D1 pore or in the overall configuration of the D1 and D2 domains of protomers A–E.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The structures of FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2 are most similar to T-20S-2 and T-20S-3a, respectively.
source: The structures of FL-20S-1 and FL-20S-2 are most similar to that of T-20S-2 (PDB ID 3J97) and T-20S-3a, respectively, with the N domains of protomers A–D and B–E interacting tightly with two adjacent αSNAPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The orientation of the SNARE complex axis relative to the D1 ring pore axis varies considerably between FL-20S and T-20S-2 structures.
source: While this core spire architecture is consistent between the FL-20S and T-20S-2 classes, superposition of the two common αSNAPs shows that the orientation of the SNARE complex axis relative to the D1 ring pore axis varies considerably (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The difference in SNARE complex orientation likely arises from the differing length of the N termini present in the truncated and full-length SNARE complexes.
source: This difference likely arises from the differing length of the N termini present in the truncated and full-length SNARE complexes, as both the FL-20S and V7-20S spires are pushed off-axis relative to the D1 pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Only two αSNAPs are present in the FL-20S reconstruction, similar to the V7-20S complex.
source: The stoichiometry of the spire structure also differs between classes. Previously, four αSNAPs were found associated with all T-20S complex classes (Zhao et al., 2015); in the case of the FL-20S reconstruction presented here, only two are present, similar to the structure of the V7-20S complex (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence of the full-length SNAP-25A linker likely interferes with binding by an additional pair of αSNAPs.
source: The presence of this SNAP-25A linker likely interferes with binding by an additional pair of αSNAPs, an observation supported by gel densitometry as well (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: In all structures of 20S complexes with full-length SNAP-25A determined to date, two rather than four bound αSNAPs are observed.
source: Furthermore, in all structures of 20S complexes with full-length SNAP-25A determined to date, two rather than four bound αSNAPs are observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Density consistent with the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A runs from the tip of the SNARE complex to the center of the D1 ring in an extended conformation at a 61.0° angle relative to the plane of the D1 ring.
source: Finally, and most important, density consistent with the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A runs from the tip of the SNARE complex to the center of the D1 ring, where it assumes an extended conformation at a 61.0° angle relative to the plane of the D1 ring (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: This is the first direct structural evidence of interaction between SNAP-25A and NSF.
source: While it has been previously speculated that SNAP-25A is the SNARE complex member upon which NSF directly acts (Cipriano et al., 2013), this is the first direct structural evidence of such an interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The spires and N domains are weak but faintly visible in the unsharpened maps of both focused reconstructions.
source: For both focused FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2 reconstructions, the spires and N domains are weak but faintly visible in the unsharpened maps
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: FL-20Sfocus-1 appears similar in configuration to the FL-20S-2 class, with N domains from protomers B–E engaged with two αSNAPs.
source: FL-20Sfocus-1 appears similar in configuration to the FL-20S-2 class, with N domains from protomers B–E engaged with two αSNAPs
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: FL-20Sfocus-2 is more similar to the FL-20S-1 class, with N domains from protomers A–D engaged.
source: while FL-20Sfocus-2 is more similar to the FL-20S-1 class, with N domains from protomers A–D engaged instead.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The two FL-20Sfocus classes differ in the relative position of the D1 ring relative to the D2 ring.
source: An additional difference between the two FL-20Sfocus classes is found in the relative position of the D1 ring relative to the D2 ring.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The two conformations of FL-20Sfocus classes are likely coupled to the N domain configurations.
source: Based on this observation and the non-hydrolyzing conditions under which the sample is prepared, the two conformations are likely coupled to the N domain configurations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the presence of ATP and absence of substrate, the D1 domains of NSF are arranged in a spiral pattern.
source: In the presence of ATP and the absence of substrate, the D1 domains of NSF are arranged in a spiral pattern, with the D1 domain of protomer A closest to the surface of its D2 domain and the D1 domain of protomer F at the top, furthest from the corresponding D2 domain (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: A pore is formed in the center of the hexamer with a highly conserved loop (the pore loop, residues 294–296, YVG) at the center.
source: A pore is formed in the center of the hexamer, with a highly conserved loop (i.e., the pore loop, 294–296, YVG) at the center.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The SNAP-25A N-terminal residues are present within the pore in an extended conformation reminiscent of a β-strand.
source: The SNAP-25A N-terminal residues are present within this pore in an extended conformation reminiscent of a β-strand with side chain density and close packing with NSF, enabling identification of the register in the density maps (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of SNAP-25A substrate leads to remodeling of the pore loops, with conformational change arising through rearrangement of tyrosine 294.
source: The presence of the SNAP-25A substrate leads to remodeling of the pore loops, with a majority of the conformational change arising through rearrangement of a highly conserved amino acid residue, tyrosine 294.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the presence of substrate, each tyrosine 294 flips up and away from the pore axis, forming a spiral pattern.
source: In the absence of substrate, each tyrosine adopts a different conformation as assessed by comparison with the cryo-EM structure of NSF alone (Zhao et al., 2015), but in the presence of substrate, each tyrosine flips up and away from the pore axis, forming a spiral pattern (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: For protomers B–D, each tyrosine Cδ1 atom intercalates nonspecifically into every other space between amino acid side chains of the substrate.
source: In the case of protomers B–D, each tyrosine Cδ1 atom intercalates nonspecifically into every other space between amino acid side chains of the substrate and is engaged in a stereotyped hydrogen bonding interaction with the nearest substrate carbonyl (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Each tyrosine 294 is engaged in a stereotyped hydrogen bonding interaction with the nearest substrate carbonyl.
source: In the case of protomers B–D, each tyrosine Cδ1 atom intercalates nonspecifically into every other space between amino acid side chains of the substrate and is engaged in a stereotyped hydrogen bonding interaction with the nearest substrate carbonyl (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: When the D1 large subdomains are superimposed, the pore loop conformations of protomers B–E are nearly identical.
source: When the D1 large subdomains are superimposed, the pore loop conformations of protomers B–E are nearly identical, while protomer A is relatively closer to the D2 ring (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Mutation of Y294 to leucine reduces disassembly of SNARE complex by 88% per unit time.
source: For NSF, a somewhat conservative pore loop mutation (Y294L) reduces disassembly of SNARE complex by 88% per unit time, while a more pronounced mutation (Y294A) reduces disassembly even further, by 94%—both significant changes relative to wild type (p<0.01) and, in the case of Y294A, nearly statistically indistinguishable from uninitiated reaction with wild type NSF (p=0.06; Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Mutation of Y294 to alanine reduces disassembly of SNARE complex by 94% per unit time.
source: For NSF, a somewhat conservative pore loop mutation (Y294L) reduces disassembly of SNARE complex by 88% per unit time, while a more pronounced mutation (Y294A) reduces disassembly even further, by 94%—both significant changes relative to wild type (p<0.01) and, in the case of Y294A, nearly statistically indistinguishable from uninitiated reaction with wild type NSF (p=0.06; Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Y294 mutations do not affect the intrinsic rate of ATP hydrolysis.
source: These mutations do not affect the intrinsic rate of ATP hydrolysis as measured by an ATPase activity assay (see Materials and methods; wild type, 28 ± 4 ATP min−1; Y294L, 26 ± 2 ATP min−1; Y294A, 31 ± 5 ATP min−1; p>0.05 for both)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Y294 mutations do not disrupt the formation of stable hexamer.
source: nor do they disrupt the formation of stable hexamer, suggesting that—as in other AAA+ proteins—the pore loops and the Y294 side chains in particular are essential to the mechanical action of NSF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The pore loops and Y294 side chains are essential to the mechanical action of NSF.
source: nor do they disrupt the formation of stable hexamer, suggesting that—as in other AAA+ proteins—the pore loops and the Y294 side chains in particular are essential to the mechanical action of NSF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Truncation of the first 16 residues of SNAP-25A slightly increased the rate of SNARE complex disassembly in vitro by 15%.
source: Surprisingly, this truncation slightly increased the rate of SNARE complex disassembly in vitro by 15% as determined by fluorescence dequenching (p<0.01) (Figure 10) and SDS-PAGE (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: SNAP-25A remains the likely candidate for engagement despite the truncated N-terminus.
source: Given the size of the syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 N-terminal domains, SNAP-25A remains the likely candidate for engagement despite the truncated N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The result implies primary sequence promiscuity in disassembly.
source: This result implies primary sequence promiscuity in disassembly and is consistent with previous observations in which NSF disassembles different SNARE complexes at similar rates (Cipriano et al., 2013; Vivona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The observed promiscuity supports the idea that NSF must disassemble a variety of SNARE complexes in different trafficking contexts in vivo.
source: More generally, this observed promiscuity supports the idea that NSF must disassemble a variety of SNARE complexes in different trafficking contexts in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The disassembly process likely proceeds without active engagement by a secondary pore loop in the D1 domain.
source: The disassembly process likely proceeds without active engagement by a secondary pore loop in the D1 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The secondary pore loop (residues 338–345, GSMAGSTG) in the large subdomain was unresolved in previous EM structures of NSF.
source: In previous EM structures of NSF, this flexible secondary pore loop (residues 338–345, GSMAGSTG) in the large subdomain was unresolved (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: In the FL-20Sfocus classes, the secondary pore loop is present in some subunits and packed to varying degrees against the substrate.
source: Here, in the FL-20Sfocus classes, this loop is present in some subunits and packed to varying degrees against the substrate (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The secondary pore loop interaction appears degenerate, with different loop residues contacting substrate in various locations.
source: Unlike the primary pore loop, this interaction appears degenerate; different loop residues contact substrate in various locations, suggesting a role in guiding the incoming substrate and/or preventing non-productive interactions with the interior surface of the D1 ring.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nucleotide occupancies of the D1 ring in FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2 are consistent with a structure poised to disassemble substrate.
source: The nucleotide occupancies of the D1 ring in the FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2 maps are consistent with a structure poised to disassemble substrate, in which protomers B–D are ATP-bound (Figure 11A, Figure 11—figure supplement 1), and key amino acids are in place to catalyze hydrolysis (Wendler et al., 2012) (despite the absence of Mg2+ under the non-hydrolyzing conditions of the sample preparation [Figure 11C–E]).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Protomers B–D are ATP-bound in the FL-20Sfocus structures.
source: The nucleotide occupancies of the D1 ring in the FL-20Sfocus-1 and FL-20Sfocus-2 maps are consistent with a structure poised to disassemble substrate, in which protomers B–D are ATP-bound (Figure 11A, Figure 11—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Nucleotide densities associated with the D1 domains of protomers A and E are ambiguous.
source: Nucleotide densities associated with the D1 domains of protomers A and E are ambiguous (Figure 11B,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11B,F.

claim: Weak density for protomer F is consistent with a nucleotide-free state.
source: Finally, weak density for protomer F is consistent with a nucleotide-free state as observed in the ATP-bound, substrate-free cryo-EM structure of NSF (Zhao et al., 2015), but nucleotide may nevertheless be present.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The substrate-bound D1 ring is quite similar to the ATP-bound, substrate-free NSF structure (D1 all-atom RMSD = 1.2 Å2).
source: The D1 ring is quite similar to that this structure (D1 all-atom RMSD = 1.2 Å2; PDB 3J94).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Structures of related AAA+ proteins engaged with protein substrate show substrate engaged by ATPase pore loops at the center of a spiral-shaped hexamer.
source: Structures of a number of related AAA+ proteins engaged with protein substrate are available—VAT (Ripstein et al., 2017), HSP104 (Gates et al., 2017), ClpB (Deville et al., 2017), Vps4 (Han et al., 2017), YME1 (Puchades et al., 2017), and TRIP13 (Alfieri et al., 2018). As in the case of NSF, each structure shows substrate engaged by ATPase pore loops at the center of a spiral-shaped hexamer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: AAA+ pore loops are distinguished by the presence of an apical aromatic amino acid—tyrosine or tryptophan—which intercalates into every other space between side chains of the substrate.
source: These pore loops are distinguished by the presence of an apical aromatic amino acid—tyrosine or tryptophan—which intercalates into every other space between side chains of the substrate, gripping it and helping to maintain it in an extended β-strand conformation within the pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: A processive, 'hand-over-hand' model for translocation in AAA+ proteins has been proposed based on structural observations.
source: The recurrent observation of this structural pattern has led to the proposal of a processive, 'hand-over-hand' model for translocation in AAA+ in which substrate is presumably pulled further into the pore in a coordinated manner with hydrolysis of ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The generalized hand-over-hand model is consistent with initial substrate loading in the absence of hydrolysis.
source: Based on our structures, we propose that this generalized hand-over-hand model is consistent with initial substrate loading in the absence of hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the absence of Mg2+, NSF-mediated disassembly of SNARE complexes was not observed by multiple independent assays.
source: Indeed, in the absence of Mg2+, NSF-mediated disassembly of SNARE complexes was not observed by multiple independent assays (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: This observation suggests that catalysis is not required for initial engagement of substrate.
source: This observation suggests that catalysis is not required for initial engagement of substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The proposal of hydrolysis-free substrate loading is corroborated by other structures of AAA+ proteins where only very limited or no nucleotide hydrolysis could have occurred.
source: More generally, our proposal of hydrolysis-free substrate loading is also corroborated by the other structures of AAA+ proteins noted above, where only very limited or no nucleotide hydrolysis could have occurred.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: No related, catalytically active AAA+ protein structure has been determined in the presence of substrate under hydrolyzing conditions.
source: In summary, no related, catalytically active AAA+ protein structure has thus far been determined in the presence of substrate under hydrolyzing conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The binding of SNAP-25A N-terminal residues likely involves a conformational change because these residues are otherwise α-helical starting at residue seven.
source: This notion is supported by the observation that the binding of the SNAP-25A N-terminal residues likely involves a conformational change because the SNAP-25A N-terminal residues are otherwise α-helical starting at residue seven as assessed by a crystal structure lacking crystal packing contacts in this region (PDB ID 5W5D) (Zhou et al., 2015b); these same residues are extended in the FL-20S complexes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Breathing motions of the D1 ring might allow the substrate to pass into the pore at the seam.
source: Given the conformational heterogeneity observed for the large subdomain of the final, highest protomer F of the D1 ring—which does not engage the substrate—and the solvent-oriented configuration of the lowest (first) protomer A, it is plausible that breathing motions of the ring might allow the substrate to pass into the pore at the seam.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Loading of the SNARE substrate by the D1 pore of NSF would likely be an important factor to stimulate ATPase activity.
source: It is likely that loading of the SNARE substrate by the D1 pore of NSF would be an important factor to stimulate ATPase activity (Cipriano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Complete threading of SNARE substrate through NSF is unlikely as the D2 domain pore is occluded in both ATP- and ADP-bound states.
source: Upon subsequent ATP hydrolysis, the SNARE substrate could be further threaded into the D1 pore, although complete threading is unlikely as the D2 domain pore is occluded in both ATP- and ADP-bound states (Zhao et al., 2015) and palmitoylation anchors SNAP-25A to the membrane following its first SNARE motif (Greaves et al., 2009; Hess et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Palmitoylation anchors SNAP-25A to the membrane following its first SNARE motif.
source: Upon subsequent ATP hydrolysis, the SNARE substrate could be further threaded into the D1 pore, although complete threading is unlikely as the D2 domain pore is occluded in both ATP- and ADP-bound states (Zhao et al., 2015) and palmitoylation anchors SNAP-25A to the membrane following its first SNARE motif (Greaves et al., 2009; Hess et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The structures reveal key pre-disassembly states of the 20S complex in which several degenerate configurations of αSNAPs and NSF N domains position the SNARE complex for engagement by NSF D1 pore loops.
source: Together, the structures of the 20S complex presented here reveal key pre-disassembly states of the 20S complex, in which several degenerate configurations of αSNAPs and NSF N domains position the SNARE complex for engagement by the highly conserved tyrosine residues on the NSF D1 pore loops under non-hydrolyzing conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: The 2:1 αSNAP:SNARE complex interface is preserved, revealing a likely conserved, core electrostatic interaction required for general formation of the 20S complex.
source: Despite the variable participation of different N domains about the NSF hexamer, the 2:1 αSNAP:SNARE complex interface is preserved, revealing what is likely a conserved, core electrostatic interaction required for the general formation of the 20S complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: The structures provide evidence for loading of the full-length neuronal SNARE complex via the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A.
source: More important, these structures provide evidence for loading of the full-length neuronal SNARE complex via the N-terminal residues of SNAP-25A.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Complete disassembly could proceed through further translocation of the N-terminus of SNAP-25A.
source: Complete disassembly could then proceed through further translocation of the N-terminus of SNAP-25A.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Translocation would exert a pulling force on the remaining membrane-anchored SNAP-25A, likely destabilizing interactions with syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2.
source: Such translocation would exert a pulling force on the remaining membrane-anchored SNAP-25A, likely destabilizing interactions with syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: The conditions under which the 20S complex was prepared and the observed nucleotide state are consistent with a two-step disassembly mechanism in which the SNARE protein is loaded passively prior to hydrolysis and disassembly.
source: Finally, the conditions under which the 20S complex was prepared in addition to the observed nucleotide state of these structures is consistent with—but not direct evidence of—a two-step disassembly mechanism in which the SNARE protein is loaded passively prior to hydrolysis and disassembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Hexameric NSF was prepared in the presence of ATP instead of AMPPNP.
source: Two key changes were made, however. First, hexameric NSF was prepared in the presence of ATP instead of the slowly hydrolyzable analogue AMPPNP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: To prevent hydrolysis, Mg2+ was omitted from the buffer, and EDTA was included to remove any trace divalent cations.
source: Moreover, to prevent hydrolysis, Mg2+ was omitted from the buffer, and EDTA was included to remove any trace divalent cations (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The SNARE complex was prepared using nearly full-length soluble portions of rat syntaxin-1A (residues 1–256) and synaptobrevin-2 (residues 1–89), with C-terminal transmembrane segments omitted.
source: Second, the SNARE complex was prepared using the nearly full-length soluble portions of rat syntaxin-1A (residues 1–256) and synaptobrevin-2 (residues 1–89), with the C-terminal transmembrane segments omitted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Nearly full-length rat SNAP-25A (residues 1–204) was used in which the long, unstructured linker spanning the distance between the two SNARE motifs is present.
source: Additionally, nearly full-length rat SNAP-25A (residues 1–204) was used in which the long, unstructured linker spanning the distance between the two SNARE motifs is present.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.
